answers.l: OK. Also what too many APIs return for errors, with the error in the body.
Not Found. A popular myth says it's named after a room at CERN. It isn't.
Internal Server Error. The server’s way of saying something threw.
Created. Should come with a Location header pointing at the new resource.
No Content. Success with an empty body.
Moved Permanently. Browsers cache it hard, so test before you ship one.
Found. Specified to keep the method, implemented by browsers as "switch to GET." Hence 303 and 307.
Bad Request.
Unauthorized, which actually means unauthenticated.
Forbidden: we know who you are, and the answer is no.
Bad Gateway. The proxy is fine. The thing behind it isn’t.
Service Unavailable. Pair it with Retry-After.
Not Modified. The answer to If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since.
I'm a teapot. From RFC 2324, the 1998 April Fools' coffee pot protocol. It survived a 2017 push to remove it from Node.js and Go.
Too Many Requests. Added in 2012 by RFC 6585.
Gateway Timeout.
Method Not Allowed. The response must include an Allow header.
Conflict. Edit races and duplicate creates.
Unprocessable Content. Born in WebDAV, adopted by every JSON API.
Accepted. Received, will process later, no promises.
Partial Content. How video seeking and resumable downloads work, via Range requests.
Continue. Lets a client check headers before sending a big body (Expect: 100-continue).
Switching Protocols. Every WebSocket connection starts with one.
See Other. The redirect-after-POST code.
Temporary Redirect that must keep the method and body.
Permanent Redirect that keeps the method. RFC 7538, 2015.
Payment Required. "Reserved for future use" since 1997.
Not Acceptable. Content negotiation failed.
Request Timeout.
Gone. Like 404, but on purpose and forever.
Precondition Failed. Optimistic locking with If-Match.
Content Too Large.
Unsupported Media Type. Usually a missing Content-Type.
Unavailable For Legal Reasons. A nod to Fahrenheit 451. RFC 7725, 2016.
Not Implemented.
Early Hints (RFC 8297). Lets the browser preload assets while the server is still thinking.
Multi-Status. WebDAV's batch response.
Multiple Choices.
Proxy Authentication Required.
Length Required.
URI Too Long.
Range Not Satisfiable.
Expectation Failed.
Enhance Your Calm. Twitter's rate-limit code before 429 existed. Never standard.
Upgrade Required.
Precondition Required. Forces clients to send conditional requests.
Request Header Fields Too Large. Usually a cookie that kept growing.
nginx only: close the connection without sending anything.
nginx only: the client gave up before the server answered.
HTTP Version Not Supported.
Network Authentication Required. The captive portal code.
Cloudflare only: the origin sent something Cloudflare couldn't understand.
Cloudflare only: the connection to your origin timed out.
Processing. A WebDAV keep-alive, since deprecated.
Non-Authoritative Information. A proxy modified the response.
Reset Content. Tells the client to clear the form.
Already Reported. WebDAV, to avoid listing the same member twice.
IM Used. From delta encoding for HTTP (RFC 3229), which almost nobody implemented.
Use Proxy. Deprecated for security reasons.
Switch Proxy. No longer used, reserved forever.
Misdirected Request. Added for HTTP/2 connection reuse gone wrong.
Locked. WebDAV.
Failed Dependency. WebDAV.
Too Early. Guards against replayed TLS 1.3 early data.
Variant Also Negotiates. Content negotiation got stuck in a loop.
Insufficient Storage. WebDAV.
Loop Detected. WebDAV.
Bandwidth Limit Exceeded. Not standard; shared-hosting panels use it.
Not Extended. Its RFC was later moved to Historic.
Not standard. LinkedIn sends it to suspected scrapers.

traps.q: Name the HTTP status code that a popular myth says was named after a room at CERN.
traps.l: There was no room 404. The 4xx and 5xx scheme came from the HTTP design itself.

traps.q: Name the HTTP status code a server sends when an unhandled exception escapes.
